Introduction and Overview This e-book is written for students in STA258 – Statistics with Applied Probability at the University of Toronto Mississauga. Its purpose is to give you a practical feel for the ideas you meet in lectures and tutorials, showing how the mathematics of probability lets us talk sensibly about uncertainty in everyday life as well as in scientific work. Uncertainty surrounds almost everything we care about. Will tomorrow’s lecture be moved online because of a snowstorm? Can a spacecraft launch if cross-winds rise above a certain threshold? Will a new medication actually shorten recovery time once it leaves the controlled environment of a clinical trial? Each question feels different on the surface, yet the same statistical machinery helps us tackle them all. By framing an uncertain outcome as a random variable we can describe its typical behaviour, calculate the odds of unusual events and, most importantly, update those odds when new information arrives. The human mind does a rough version of this calculation all the time. We decide to carry an umbrella because dark clouds look threatening, or we leave extra time for a commute after hearing a traffic report. But gut instinct is easily misled: streaks appear in gambling even when the dice are fair, and vivid anecdotes can drown out a mountain of quieter data. Formal probability offers a sturdier foundation. If meteorologists combine radar images, satellite readings and decades of storm records, they can say not just “it might snow,” but “there is a 70 % chance of more than ten centimetres by morning.” If engineers measure how often a particular alloy fractures under stress, they can quote the lifetime of a bridge girder with a clear margin of error rather than a hopeful guess. In each case the numbers come from a sampling distribution—an imagined catalogue of results we would see if we could repeat the experiment or observation indefinitely. Throughout this book we will revisit that catalogue many times. We start by defining random variables and their distributions, then learn how to simulate, visualise and summarise those distributions with real data. From there we build the tools needed for inference: confidence intervals that put a reasonable bound around an unknown parameter; hypothesis tests that weigh the evidence for competing explanations; and regression models that let us tease out the influence of several factors at once. The tone is informal and example-driven—you will see as much reference to snowfall totals, pulse rates and exam scores as to abstract notation—yet every result rests on rigorous mathematics. By the end you should feel at home translating a messy, uncertain situation into symbols, pushing those symbols through the machinery of probability and translating the answer back into plain language someone with no statistical background can understand. That ability—to move comfortably between raw experience and quantitative insight—is what STA258 is all about, and what this e-book aims to nurture.

Chapter 1 Introduction 1.1 Foundations Masoud will proofread. Intuitively, statistics can be considered the science of uncertainty. Formally: Definition 1.1 (Statistics) Statistics is the science of collecting, classifying, summarizing, analyzing and interpreting data. In statistics, researchers are often interested in characteristics of a large group of interest. They often observe behaviours, patterns, trends etc. to give a conclusion for the group. To make the conclusions, researchers require data to support them. Definition 1.2 (Population) A population is a set of similar observations which is of interest for some experimental questions. It can be a set of existing objects such as all people in Canada, or hypothetical group of existing objects such as the set of all possible hands in a game of poker. A population can be a set of existing objects such as all people in Canada, or hypothetical group of existing objects such as the set of all possible hands in a game of poker. Populations are often large. Some more examples are given below. Example 1.1 All students at the University of Toronto All residents of Mississauga Data collection from every object in a population is often not feasible to perform. Researchers often select a finite number of observations to study. Definition 1.3 (Sample) A sample refers to a subset from population. Example 1.2 A random sample of 50 students at the University of Toronto. A random sample of 100 residents of Mississauga. Definition 1.4 (Unit) The objects within a sample for which data are collected. Example 1.3 In a sample of 10 students, a unit would be one of the students in this sample. There are characteristics of a population and sample which are of interest to us. Definition 1.5 (Parameter) A parameter is a numerical quantity of a population which summarizes a characteristic of the population. Some examples of parameters are introduced in this section. These terms will be discussed in more detail in later chapters. Example 1.4 Population mean \(\mu\) Population standard deviation \(\sigma\) Population proportion \(p\) The true value of a parameter is usually unknown since it is extremely difficult to take measurements on every unit in a population. Therefore we often use measurements from a sample to estimate the value of a parameter. Definition 1.6 (Statistic) A statistic is a numerical quantity of a sample which summarizes a characteristic of the sample. Since we have control over a sample, the numerical values of statistics are often calculated and known. Some examples of statistics are given below and similar to the parameters in 1.4, these terms will also be discussed in more detail in later chapters. Example 1.5 Sample mean \(\bar{x}\) Sample standard deviation \(s\) Sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) Statistics can be broken down into two broad categories: descriptive statistics and inferential statistics which are given in definitions 1.7 and 1.8 below. Definition 1.7 (Descriptive Statistics) Descriptive statistics are numerical and graphical methods used to analyze, interpret, and represent data. Definition 1.8 (Inferential Statistics) Inferential statistics use information from a sample to make generalizations about a larger population. 1.2 Types of data Data can be classified into two main categories: quantitative and qualitative data. Definition 1.9 (Quantitative data) Data which can be measured numerically. Example 1.6 Height weight Age Temperature Definition 1.10 (Qualitative data) Data which can not be measured numerically. Qualitative data falls into categories instead. Example 1.7 Favourite colour out of red, green, blue Favourite flavour of ice-cream out of chocolate, vanilla, strawberry 1.3 Introduction to Inferential statistics As discussed in Section 1.1, we mentioned that the numerical values of parameters are usually unknown, however the numerical values of statistics are calculated and known. We also quantify our confidence that the statistic is representative of the parameter and use statistics to test hypotheses about the population parameters.
